meta.title: Ocean Explorer
meta.description: Ocean Explorer: dive from the surface to the deepest trench.

descent.label: The descent
descent.title: Breaking the surface
descent.text: The sky folds into a ripple of light overhead. With every metre, the sea takes a little more of the sun.
descent.textNight: The night sky folds into a ripple of silver overhead. Below you, the water is already dark.

shallows.label: Shallow water
shallows.title: Cathedral light
shallows.text: Shafts of sun lean through the blue. Red light is long gone; below 200 metres only blue still reaches you.
shallows.textNight: Faint moonbeams lean through the dark blue. Here and there, plankton sparks as you pass.

glow.label: Bioluminescence
glow.title: Living light
glow.text: Out of the dark, jellyfish pulse with their own light. Most animals down here make it: to hunt, to hide, to find each other.

whale.label: Whale encounter
whale.title: A passing giant
whale.text: A sperm whale hunts in total darkness, finding squid by sound alone. One breath at the surface lasts it over an hour.

vents.label: Hydrothermal vents
vents.title: Black smokers
vents.text: Water hotter than 350 °C pours out of the seafloor, thick with minerals. Life thrives here without any sunlight at all.

abyss.label: The abyss
abyss.title: The abyss
abyss.text: The deepest water on Earth, under more than a thousand times the pressure of the air above. Something vast moves at the edge of the light, and is gone.

return.label: Return to surface
return.title: Back into the light
return.text: Eleven kilometres of water above you, and every metre a little brighter than the last.

end.title: The ocean is still unexplored
end.note: More than eighty percent of the ocean has never been mapped, observed or explored.

card.name: Megalodon
card.legend: Confirmed: known from the fossil record. Estimate: calculated by scientists, given as a range. Hypothesis: a leading explanation that is still debated.

length.label: Length
length.value: About 15–20 m for large adults; some studies suggest the largest exceeded 20 m. Worked out from teeth and vertebrae: no complete skeleton is known.

weight.label: Weight
weight.value: Tens of tonnes. One 2022 3D reconstruction put a 16 m shark at about 61 t; other estimates differ widely.

period.label: Period
period.value: Early Miocene to early Pliocene, roughly 23 to 3.6 million years ago

habitat.label: Habitat and range
habitat.value: Warm and temperate seas worldwide, from coastal shelves to the open ocean. Its teeth are found on every continent except Antarctica.

diet.label: Diet
diet.value: A top predator of large prey: whales and other marine mammals, and large fish. Bite marks on fossil whale bones show it.

facts.f1: It is known almost only from teeth and vertebrae: a shark’s skeleton is cartilage, which rarely fossilises.
facts.f2: Its teeth are triangular and serrated, and can be more than 17 cm long: among the largest of any shark.
facts.f3: The chemistry of its tooth enamel (a 2023 study) suggests it was partly warm-blooded, about 7 °C warmer than the water around it.
facts.f4: Young megalodons seem to have grown up in warm, shallow coastal nurseries; one was identified in Panama.
facts.f5: Why it died out is still debated: cooling seas, changes in its prey and competition, possibly with the great white shark.
facts.f6: Its exact shape is unknown. Recent studies (2024–2025) suggest a more slender body than older reconstructions modelled on the great white.
facts.f7: It was not the ancestor of the great white shark: the two belong to different families.

card.note: The shark shown is an artistic reconstruction: what the megalodon really looked like is unknown. This dive shows it in the deep; the fossils show it lived mostly in the upper waters of warm coastal and open seas.
